parole.significato: -itis, a suffix denoting inflammation of the affixed organ.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -ῖτις (-îtis).

parole.significato: denotes a relationship with a place, building, etc
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek -εῖον (-eîon). Often found already in ancient words, or used to create new modern terms.

parole.significato: Used to form a reproductive numeral (adjective) from a cardinal number.
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -πλάσιος (-plásios), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥-h₂-t-yo-s, from *pel- (“to fold”).
From Ancient Greek -τος (-tos), from Proto-Indo-European *-tós.
From Ancient Greek -τρια (-tria), from Proto-Indo-European *-trih₂.

parole.significato: eating the food denoted by the prefix
parole.testo: Inherited from Ancient Greek -φάγος (-phágos).
From Ancient Greek ἄκρα (ákra), from the feminine of ἄκρος (ákros), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós.
From Ancient Greek ἄλγος (álgos).
From Ancient Greek ἄνεμος (ánemos), Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, a nominal derivative of *h₂enh₁- (“breathe”).
Learnedly, from Ancient Greek ἄργῠρος (árgŭros, “silver”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂erǵ-.
From Ancient Greek ἄριστος (áristos, “best, noblest”).
Probably a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἄροτρον (árotron), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érh₃trom. Doublet of αλέτρι (alétri), inherited through a diminutive form.

parole.significato: the augment, a prefix marking indicative past tenses (occurs only in stressed position)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἐ- (e-), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁é-. Cognate with Sanskrit अ- (á-), Phrygian ε- (e-).
From Ancient Greek ἕλιξ (hélix), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn”). Doublet of έλικας (élikas).
From Ancient Greek ἔργον (érgon), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom.

From Ancient Greek ἔρχομαι (érkhomai, “I go”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ergʰ- (“to move, go”). The meaning shift and the perfective forms are from the suppletive aorist ἦλθον (êlthon, “I came”) (with regular shift λθ > ρθ). Compare also the Albanian form erdha (“I came”).
From Ancient Greek ἤρεμος (ḗremos), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rem- (“to rest”).

parole.significato: to fly, rise into the air
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek ἵπταμαι (híptamai), late metathetic form of Ancient Greek πέτομαι (pétomai) from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti (“to fly”) from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”).

parole.significato: a-, an-, in-, un-, -less (Τhe alpha privative, privative a, alpha privativum, indicating an opposite or lacking sense)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-), from Proto-Indo-European *n̥-.

From Byzantine Greek αἷμα (haîma) / αἷμαν (haîman, “blood”), from Ancient Greek αἷμα (haîma, “blood”), which is of ultimately uncertain and highly contested origin (see Ancient Greek lemma for various proposed derivations from Proto-Indo-European or Northwest Semitic languages).

parole.significato: egg (spherical or ellipsoidal body produced by birds, reptiles, insects and other animals, housing the embryo during it…
parole.testo: Back-formation from the plural αβγά (avgá), itself extracted from ταβγά (tavgá, “the eggs”), a regular phonological development of Ancient Greek τά ᾠά (tá ōiá): :τά ᾠά /ta.oˈa/ → *τα ωγά /ta.oˈɣa/ → [tawγá] /tau̯ˈɣa/ → ταβγά /tavˈɣa/. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ōwyóm via Proto-Hellenic *
From Ancient Greek αἰτία (aitía).

From Byzantine Greek ἁλάτιν (halátin), from Koine Greek ἁλάτιον (halátion), a diminutive of Ancient Greek ἅλας (hálas), from ἅλς (háls), from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂l-, *sḗh₂l. Compare the borrowed doublet άλας (álas) and Mariupol Greek а́лас (álas).
Inherited from Ancient Greek ἀνάγκη (anánkē, “necessity”).
From Ancient Greek ἀπό (apó, “from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, away”).
Inherited from Ancient Greek ἀμέλγω (amélgō), with rhotacism and metathesis; from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-.
Inherited from Byzantine Greek ἀστέριν (astérin), from Hellenistic Koine Greek ἀστέριον (astérion), diminutive of the Ancient Greek ἀστήρ (astḗr), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr.
From the Ancient Greek αὐγή (augḗ, “sunlight, dawn”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewg- (“to increase, to enlarge”).

parole.significato: pipe, flute, fife (any wind instrument played by blowing)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek αὐλός (aulós), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlos (“tube”). Cognates include Lithuanian aulas, Norwegian aul, Hittite [script needed] (auli-, “tube-shaped organ in the neck”), and perhaps also Latin alvus, Old Church Slavonic улица (ulica, “small lane, narrow street”), and Old Arme
From Ancient Greek ὀμφαλός (omphalós), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃m̥bʰ-, a variant of *h₃nebʰ-. Doublet of ομφαλός (omfalós).

Back-formation from the plural αφτιά (aftiá), extracted from article & noun τ’ αφτιά (t’ aftiá, “the ears”), from Byzantine Greek τά ἀφτία (tá aphtía) (singular τό ἀφτίον (tó aphtíon)), from Koine Greek τά ὠτία (tá ōtía) (singular ὠτίον (ōtíon)), diminutive of Ancient Greek τᾰ̀ ὦτᾰ (tằ ôtă) (singula
From Ancient Greek ἐχῖνος (ekhînos), with stress shift, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁eǵʰis.
From Proto-Indo-European *bʰelH- (“white”). Cognate with Proto-Slavic *bolto (“swamp”), Romanian baltă (“mud, swamp”) and Albanian baltë (“mud”). Often considered an Illyrian substratum word.

parole.significato: base, foundation (the lowest part of something)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek βάσις (básis), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis.
From Ancient Greek βέλος (bélos), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷélHos, from *gʷelH-.
Inherited from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos).
From βαλανίδι (valanídi), from a diminutive of Ancient Greek βάλανος (bálanos), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷelh₂-.

Inherited from Ancient Greek βλάξ (bláx, “soft”) from the accusative singular τὸν (tòn) βλάκα (bláka), from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“soft, weak, tender”) (through *μλάξ [mláx] > *μβλάξ [mbláx]). Cognates include Latin mollis (“soft, mild”), Sanskrit मृदु (mṛdú, “soft, mild, weak”) and English mil
From Ancient Greek βρέφος (bréphos), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷrebʰ-.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek βραδύς (bradús).
From Ancient Greek βροντή (brontḗ).

From Byzantine Greek βυζίον (buzíon), from βυζάνω (buzánō, “to breastfeed”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to swell, bend, curve”). From Ancient Greek γάλα (gála), from Proto-Indo-European *glakt-, *galakt-. Cognate with Mariupol Greek га́ла (hála).
Inherited from Ancient Greek γάμος (gámos), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem- (“to marry”). Compare Mariupol Greek га́мус (hámus).
Inherited from Byzantine Greek γαμπρός (gamprós), form of γαμβρός (gambrós), from Ancient Greek γαμβρός (gambrós), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.
With ending -άω to γελώ (geló) in the pattern of 3rd person -άει. From Byzantine Greek γελῶ (gelô), from Ancient Greek γελῶ (gelô), contracted form of γελάω (geláō), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵelh₂-.

From Ancient Greek γοητεία (goēteía, “charm, jugglery, sorcery”), from Ancient Greek γόης (góēs, “sorcerer, wizard”), from Ancient Greek γοάω (goáō, “to groan, bewail”), perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *geh₃- (“to sing, cry”) or Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, invoke, cry out”).
From Ancient Greek δαίω (daíō).
From Ancient Greek δάκρυ (dákru), from Proto-Indo-European *dáḱru-.
From Ancient Greek δίκη (díkē).

The earlier form is δίδω (dído) with metaplasm to -νω (-no), from Byzantine Greek δίδω (dídō), from Ancient Greek δίδωμι (dídōmi), from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, reduplicated present of *deh₃- (“to give”).
From Ancient Greek δομή (domḗ), from Proto-Indo-European *doméh₂, from the root *dem- (“to build”).

From Ancient Greek δρέπω (drépō), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to tear, pluck”), related to Proto-Slavic *drapati (“to scratch”). Less certain is the relation with Proto-Germanic *trabō (“fringe”) and Medieval Latin drappus.

From Ancient Greek δυσ- (dus-) + λέξις (léxis, “diction”, “word”), from Ancient Greek λέγω (légō, “to speak”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leg- (“to collect, gather; to speak”). The term was coined with λέξις (léxis) being taken to mean "reading," likely due to semantic conflation of Greek
From Ancient Greek δώδεκα (dṓdeka), from Proto-Indo-European *dwoΗdeḱm̥. Cognate with Mariupol Greek дъо́дъэка (ðóðeka), дъо́дъека (ðóðjeka).
From Ancient Greek εἰλεός (eileós).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐλέγχω (elénkhō).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐν (en).
From Ancient Greek ἐνενήκοντα (enenḗkonta), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
From Ancient Greek ἐνυδρίς (enudrís), of ultimately the same Proto-Indo-European origin as the synonym βίδρα (vídra).

From Byzantine Greek ἑξήντα (hexḗnta), from Ancient Greek ἑξήκοντα (hexḗkonta), from Proto-Indo-European *sweḱsḱomth₂, from the earlier *swéḱs-dḱomt-h₂ (“six-ten”). Compare Mariupol Greek кси́нда (ksínda).
From Byzantine Greek ἐσύ (esú), from Ancient Greek σύ (sú), from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.
From Ancient Greek ἑταιρεία (hetaireía, “association, brotherhood”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”).

From Byzantine Greek ζευγάρι (zeugári), ζευγάριν (zeugárin), from ζευγάριον (zeugárion), diminutive of Ancient Greek ζεῦγος (zeûgos). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to join, tie together”).
From Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “belt; loins, waist”).

parole.significato: uncle (a parent’s brother or parent's brother-in-law)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-. Compare to θειος (theios).
From Ancient Greek θεσμός (thesmós), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put”).
From Ancient Greek θυγάτηρ (thugátēr), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰugh₂tḗr. Cognate with Tsakonian σάτη (sáti).

From ίπταμαι (íptamai, “to fly”), learned from Koine Greek ἵπταμαι (híptamai), late form of Ancient Greek πέτομαι (pétomai), from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti (“to fly”) from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”).
From Ancient Greek κᾰλός (“beautiful, morally beautiful, of good quality”), from Proto-Indo-European *kal-wo-s, form of *kal- (“beautiful”).
From Byzantine Greek, with synizesis to avoid hiatus, from Ancient Greek καρδία (kardía), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱḗr. Cognate with Italiot Greek cardia, Mariupol Greek кардъи́я (karðíja).
From Ancient Greek κενός (kenós), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱen-.

Inherited from Byzantine Greek κεφάλιν (kephálin), from Hellenistic Koine Greek κεφάλιον (kephálion, “little head”), diminutive of the Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ-. Doublet of κεφαλή (kefalí).
From Ancient Greek κλάω (kláō, “to break”) with addition of a nasal infix. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”). Related to κλάσμα (klásma, “fraction”).
From Ancient Greek κοινός (koinós), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“with”).

From Ancient Greek κωφός (kōphós), which, if related to κηφήν (kēphḗn, “drone, lazy vagabond”), is possibly from Proto-Indo-European *k/gʰ(e/o)h₂bʰ-, but without any other IE cognates; both could be from Pre-Greek.
From Koine Greek κράτησις (krátēsis), from Ancient Greek κρατέω (kratéō), ultimately from κράτος (krátos) and Proto-Indo-European *kret- (“insight, strength”).
From Ancient Greek κράτος (krátos, “might, power”), from Proto-Indo-European *kret-.

parole.significato: link, ring (attached to or part of a chain)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κρίκος (kríkos); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“bend, turn”).
From Ancient Greek κόπρος (kópros).

From Ancient Greek λαγώς (lagṓs), from λαγωός (lagōós), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg- (“to droop, be slack, languid”) in the sense of drooping ears; see also Latin langueō and languidus, Ancient Greek λαγγάζω (langázō, “to slacken”) and λάγνος (lágnos, “lascivious, lustful”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek λοβός m (lobós), from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂b- (“to hang loosely”).
From Byzantine Greek λούζω, from Ancient Greek λούω (loúō, “to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃-.

parole.significato: rabies (animal and human disease caused by species of Lyssavirus)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek λύσσα (lússa), from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos (“wolf”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek μέγας, from Proto-Indo-European *méǵh₂s (“great”).
From Ancient Greek μέλι (méli), from Proto-Indo-European *mélid. Compare Mariupol Greek мел (mjel).
Inherited from Ancient Greek μένω (ménō), from Proto-Indo-European *men-.
From Ancient Greek μήν (mḗn), from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s. Compare Mariupol Greek ми́на (mína).
From Ancient Greek μαστός (mastós).
From Ancient Greek μηχᾰνή (mēkhănḗ).
Inherited from Ancient Greek μῑκρο- (mīkro-, “small”).
Inherited from Ancient Greek μῑκρός (mīkrós, “small, insignificant”).
From Ancient Greek μύξα (múxa, “mucus”), which shares an origin with μύκης (múkēs, “fungus, mushroom”), from Proto-Indo-European *mew-k- (“slip, slime”). Cognates include Latin mucus.
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek νᾱῦς (nāûs, “ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us. Cognate with Italian nave, Persian ناو (nâv).
From Ancient Greek νεκρός (nekrós).
From Byzantine Greek νύχιν (núkhin), inherited from Ancient Greek ὀνύχιον (onúkhion), diminutive of ὄνυξ (ónux), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-.

Inherited from Byzantine Greek νύχτα (núkhta), form of νύκτα (núkta) from Ancient Greek νύξ (núx), as in the accusative singular νύκτα (núkta), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts. Cognate with Mariupol Greek ны́хта (nýxta).

parole.significato: to card, comb (stage in fibre production)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ξαίνω (xaínō), from Proto-Indo-European *ksen- (“to scratch; to comb, card”), from *késr̥ (“comb”), from the root *kes-. Possible cognates include Latin sentis (“thorn”), Irish cíor (“comb”), English hair.
From Ancient Greek ὀγδοήκοντα (ogdoḗkonta), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ὀξύς (oxús).
From Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos.
From Ancient Greek ὀστέον (ostéon), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃esth₁-, *h₃osth₁-. Compare Mariupol Greek студъ (stuð).
From Ancient Greek οὖρον (oûron, “urine”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wers- (“to rain, drip”), *weh₁r-.
From Byzantine Greek πάντα (pánta), from Ancient Greek πάντα (pánta), accusative of πᾶς (pâs, “whole”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂nts; cf. also παν (pan). Cognate with Pontic Greek πάντα (pánta).

From Ancient Greek πέλεκυς (pélekus), cognate with Sanskrit परशु (paraśú, “axe”), which would reflect Proto-Indo-European *peleḱús if reconstructed back to PIE. Beekes suggested a Pre-Greek origin. Compare also German Beil (“axe”) as well as Hungarian and Turkish balta, both meaning "axe."
From Ancient Greek παστός (pastós), from πάσσω (pássō, “sprinkle”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₁t- (“to shake”).

From Ancient Greek πελώριος (pelṓrios, “enormous”), from πέλωρ (pélōr, “supernatural monster”), of unknown origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *kʷer-ōr modified by dissimilation, given variant forms such as τέλωρ (télōr) and τελώριος (telṓrios) which point to an original initial *kʷ, though thi
From Ancient Greek πεντήκοντα (pentḗkonta), from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷēḱomth₂, from earlier *pénkʷedḱomt (“fifty”).

From πετ(ώ) (pet(ó)) + modern suffix -άω (-áo). From Koine Greek πετῶ (petô), contracted form of πετάω (petáō) from Ancient Greek πέταμαι (pétamai), from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti (“to fly”) from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”).
Inherited from Ancient Greek πετεινός (peteinós) from πέτομαι (pétomai, “to fly”) from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πιέζω (piézō). Doublet of πιάνω (piáno).

parole.significato: to wash (your body, dishes, clothes, car, etc)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πλύνω (plúnō), from Proto-Indo-European *plew- (“to wash”).
From Ancient Greek πλήρης (plḗrēs), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-, pleh₁-r-. Compare Latin plērus.
From Ancient Greek ποῖος (poîos), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís.

From Ancient Greek πολῐορκέω (polĭorkéō, “to besiege, blockade”) (from πόλις (pólis, “city”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tpelH- (“city; fortification”)) + ἕρκος (hérkos, “enclosure; fence”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *serḱ- (“to emend, make good, recompense”))) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós,
From Ancient Greek πορθμεῖον (porthmeîon), from πορθμός (porthmós), from περάω (peráō)/περῶ (perô), from πέρα (péra), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“to carry forth”).

parole.significato: foal (infant or young horse, donkey or mule)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek πουλάριν (poulárin), from Ancient Greek πωλάριον (pōlárion), diminutive form of πῶλος (pôlos), from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂uros, from *peh₂w-.
From Ancient Greek ποῦ (poû), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷos.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain, possibly from Proto-Slavic *buca (“bulge, protrusion”). Compare Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to stick, stab”), which is of uncertain origin. Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bud- (“to shoot, sprout”), itself speculated to be of substrate origin.
From Ancient Greek πρός (prós), from Proto-Indo-European *próti ~ *préti.

parole.significato: burette, glass laboratory instrument used for titration
parole.testo: Katharevousa learned borrowing from Koine Greek προχοΐς (prokhoḯs, “chamber pot”), diminutive of Ancient Greek πρόχους (prókhous, “ewer, wine jug”) by semantic influence of the latter; itself from προ- (pro-) + χοῦς (khoûs, “measure of liquid capacity”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-.

From Ancient Greek πτηνός (ptēnós, “flying, winged creature, bird”), from πέτομαι (pétomai), itself from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂eti (“to fly”) from the root *peth₂- (literally “to spread one’s wings”). parole.significato: leg (portion of the lower human appendage from the thigh to the ankle)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek πόδιν (pódin), from Ancient Greek πόδιον (pódion), diminutive of πούς, ποδός (poús, podós), from Proto-Indo-European *póds, *pṓds.
From Ancient Greek πότε (póte), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷokʷe, from *kʷos + *-kʷe, equivalent to πο- (po-) + τε (te).
Learnedly, from Ancient Greek ῥεῦμα (rheûma), from ῥέω (rhéō), from Proto-Indo-European *srew- (“to flow”). Compare to ρέμα n (réma, “stream”).

Inherited from Byzantine Greek σαράντα (saránta), from Ancient Greek τεσσαράκοντα (tessarákonta), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwr̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *kʷetwr̥-dḱomt (“four-ten”). From Ancient Greek σεμνός (semnós, “revered, august, holy”), from σέβομαι (sébomai, “I feel awe”), from Proto-Indo-European *tyegʷ- (“avoid, yield to”).
From Ancient Greek, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *skeh₂iwo-. Cognate with Latin scaevus.

Learned borrowing from Koine Greek σκελετός (skeletós, “skeleton”), ancient sense: "dried up, dried up body, withered", from σκελε- (skele-) (found at σκέλλω (skéllō, “dry, dry up, make dry, parch”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelh₁- (“to parch, wither”)) + -ετός (-etós). From Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ, “theatre stage”).
Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σορός (sorós), from Proto-Indo-European *tworHos, from *twerH- (“to enclose”).
From Ancient Greek σπῶ (spô) / σπάω (spáō) + -άζω (-ázo), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peh₂- (“to draw, set in motion”). Also see σπάω (spáo).

parole.significato: alternative form of σπάζω (spázo) (active voice only)
parole.testo: From Byzantine Greek σπῶ (spô) / σπάω (spáō), from Ancient Greek σπάω (spáō), of Proto-Indo-European origin. Also see σπάζω (spázo).
From Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra), from Proto-Indo-European *sper- (“to twist, turn”).
From Ancient Greek σταθμός (stathmós), from Proto-Indo-European *sth₂-dʰ-mós.
From Ancient Greek σταυρός (staurós), from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”).

From Ancient Greek στερεός (stereós), from Proto-Indo-European *ster- (“stiff”). Cognate with Latin stultus, stolidus, sterilis, strēnuus, stīria. See also Old English steorfan (“to die”), Latin torpeō, Lithuanian tirpstu (“to become rigid”), and Old Church Slavonic трупети (trupeti).
From Ancient Greek στλεγγίς (stlengís, “strigil”), from Proto-Indo-European *streng-.

From Ancient Greek στόμα (stóma), from Proto-Indo-European *stomn̥, *stomen- (“mouth, muzzle”).

Inherited from Ancient Greek σύζυγος (súzugos, “mate, yoked together”), from συ(ν) (su(n), “together”) + ζυγός (zugós, “yoke, pair”), from Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (“to join, tie together”). Cognate with English syzygy, itself a borrowing from the related συζυγία (suzugía, “union, junction”).

From Ancient Greek τρίβω (tríbō).
From Ancient Greek τρίζω (trízō), from the same imitative Proto-Indo-European root as Latin strido (“to screech, grate”).
From Koine Greek τριάντα (triánta), from Ancient Greek τριάκοντα (triákonta), from Proto-Indo-European *tridḱómt (“thirty”).
From Ancient Greek τρόμος (trómos, “trembling, quaking, quivering”), from Proto-Indo-European *trem- (“to tremble”). Compare Mariupol Greek тре́мус (trjémus).

From Ancient Greek ὑφαίνω (huphaínō), from Proto-Indo-European *webʰ-.

From Ancient Greek φάλλαινα (phállaina), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to inflate, blow, swell”), from *bʰel- (“to bloom”). Cognates include Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon), Gothic 𐌱𐌻𐍉𐌼𐌰 (blōma), Old English blōstm, blæd (“leaf”) (English blossom, blade) and Sanskrit फुलम् (phulam).

From Byzantine Greek φίδιν (phídin), ὀφίδιν (ophídin), from Koine Greek ὀφίδιον (ophídion); diminutive of Ancient Greek ὄφις (óphis), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ógʷʰis, *h₃égʷʰis (“snake”). Cognate with Mariupol Greek фидъ (fið).
From Byzantine Greek φαγί(ν) (phagí(n)), from Ancient Greek φαγεῖν (phageîn), infinitive of ἔφαγον (éphagon), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂g-, zero-grade of *bʰeh₂g- (“to divide, distribute”).
Inherited from Ancient Greek φόβος (phóbos), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰegʷ- (“to run, to flee”).

parole.significato: leaf (of plant, etc); blade (leaf of grass, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- through a root *bʰol-yom), and semantic loan from French feuille in some senses, such as "sheet". For "playing card", semantic loan from Italian carte. Cognate with Mariupol Greek фи́лу (fílu).

From Ancient Greek χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “thousand”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰesliyoy, from *ǵʰes-.

From Ancient Greek χθές (khthés), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰǵʰyés.

From Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ).
From Ancient Greek χορός (khorós).
From Ancient Greek χρῑ́ω (khrī́ō).

Inherited from Ancient Greek ὕπνος (húpnos, “sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *supnós (“sleep”). Cognates include Mariupol Greek и́пно (ípno), English sweven, Sanskrit स्वप्न (svápna), Spanish sueño, Italian sonno and Latvian sapnis.

From Ancient Greek ῠ̔́στερος (hŭ́steros, “later”), comparative form of an unattested adjective with superlative ὕστᾰτος (hústătos, “last”) from Proto-Indo-European *údteros (“higher, outer”) from *úd (“upwards, away”) which would make it cognate with English out. Inherited from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “fixed period of time”), from Proto-Indo-European *yeh₁- (“year, season”). Cognate with Tsakonian ούρα (oúra).

Inherited from Koine Greek δαγκάνω (dankánō) with metaplasm after -ώνω (-óno) verbs. From the root of δάκνω (dáknō), from Proto-Indo-European *denḱ-. Or from Byzantine Greek δακώνω (dakṓnō), based on the ancient aorist ἔδακον (édakon), with the voicing of [k] influenced by Hellenistic Koine δαγκάνω.
